8526.t: CE6344: Transport Project Evaluation and Decision making
8526.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE6344 : Transport Project Evaluation and Decision making { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Introduction to Estimating Transportation Demand and Supply (6 hours)
Overall transportation project development, Budgeting, Financial Planning, The process of transportation project development, Models associated with transportation impact evaluation, Procedural framework for transportation systems evaluation, Demand-supply equilibration, Dynamics of transportation demand and supply, Elasticity of travel demand and supply, Classification of elasticity, Consumer surplus, and latent demand.
Module II: Transportation and Vehicle Operating Costs (8 hours)
Classification of transportation costs: Transportation agency costs, Transportation user costs, General structure and behavior of cost functions and road pricing, Vehicle Operating Costs, Road user cost study in India, Components of VOC, Factors affecting VOC, Fuel consumption relationships, Procedural framework for assessing VOC impacts.
Module III: Value of Travel Time Savings and Accident Costs (8 hours)
Categorizations of travel time, The framework for assessing travel time impacts, The economic concept of evaluation of travel time savings, Issues relating to travel time value estimation, The methodology for monetary evaluation of passenger's travel time, Review of work in India on passengers' travel time, Relevance of accident costing for a developing country, Procedural framework for safety impact evaluation, Review of alternative methodologies for accident costing, Certain issues connected with accident costing, Methods for estimating crash reduction factors, Before and after case studies.
Module IV: Economic Evaluation of Transportation Projects (8 hours)
Economic significance of transport, Performance measures in transportation evaluation, Costs and benefits of transport projects, Basic principles of economic evaluation, Elements of engineering economics, Methods of economic evaluation, Benefit-cost ratio method, First-year rate of return, Net present value method, Internal rate of return method, Comparison of the various methods of economic evaluation, Life cycle cost analysis, Case studies, Software packages for economic efficiency analysis.
Module V: Evaluation of Transportation Projects and Programs Using Multiple Criteria (6 hours)
Basic concepts, Single vs. multiple criteria, Evaluation, Decision making and optimization, Steps in multicriteria decision making, Case study: evaluation of metro rail projects using multicriteria, Financial analysis of highway project case study, PPP-based transport project case study.

Course Objective

1 .

To enable the students to be able to estimate Transportation Demand and Supply
2 .

To enable the students to be able to estimate transportation and Vehicle Operating Costs.
3 .

To enable the students to understand the value of time travel savings and accident costs.
4 .

To enable students to evaluate Transportation Projects based on various criteria.

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: The students will be able to estimate Transportation Demand and Supply.
CO2: The students will be able to learn about transportation and vehicle operating costs.
CO3: The students will be able to understand the value of time travel savings and accident costs.
CO4: The students will be able to evaluate Transportation Projects.
CO5: The students can evaluate Transportation Projects based on various criteria.

Essential Reading

1 .

P. McCarthy, Transportation Economics, Blackwell

2 .

Meyer John Robert Meyer, José A. Gómez-Ibáñez, William B. Tye, and Clifford Winston, Essays in Transportation Economics and Policy, Brookings Institution Press

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Kenneth Duncan Boyer, Principles of transportation economics, Addison-Wesley

2 .

Kumares C. Sinha, and Samuel Labi, Transportation Decision Making: Principles of Project Evaluation and Programming, Wiley

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE6431 : Advanced Fluid Mechanics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: [7 hours]
Fluid Kinematics: Velocity field, Acceleration of a fluid element, Rotation of fluid element, Stream lines and stream function, Irrotational flow, Reynolds transport theorem.
Module 2: [8 hours]
Fluid Dynamics: Euler’s equation, Integration of Euler’s equation to get Bernoulli’s equation. Application of Bernouliis equation, Conservation of mass and momentum: continuity and momentum equation,
Module 3: [8 hours]
One-dimensional Viscous Flow: Couette flow, Flow through a pipe and channel, Laminar and turbulent regimes, Navier-Stokes equations, Exact solutions for simple cases,
Module 4: [8 hours]
Boundary Layer: Boundary Layer Theory for low and high Viscosity, Boundary Layer thickness, Prandtl’s Equation, Momentum Integral Equation, Pressure Distribution in boundary layer, Flow over a flat plate, Flow through conduits, Momentum integral equation.
Module 5: [5 hours]
Dimension analysis and similarities: Buckingham pi theorem, types of similarities, forces influencing hydraulic phenomenon, significance of dimensionless numbers, distorted model, and model proto type similarity law.

Course Objective

1 .

To provide students with a sound foundation in the mathematical, scientific and engineering fundamentals necessary to formulate, solve and analyze engineering problems in Fluid Mechanics.
2 .

Ability to apply mass, momentum and energy conservation principles for fluid flow
3 .

Ability to understand and apply the knowledge regarding the boundary layer theory to the real life hydraulic structures
4 .

Understanding the application of fluid mechanics principles for practical problems

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: To have the basic understanding on fluid mechanics and Fluid Kinematics:.
CO2: To know the continuity and momentum equation in fluid dynamics.
CO3: Relates the basic theory of laminar and turbulent flow with application of fluid mechanics.
CO4: To Calculate and determine the effect of boundary layer on solid body.
CO5: Understand the basic concepts of Dimension analysis and similarities in fluid mechanics.

K. Subramanya, Theory and application of Fluid Mechanics, Tata Mc Graw hill, New Delhi

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CY3102 : Bio-organic Chemistry { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1
Carbohydrates: Classification, Monosaccharides, erythroabdthreodiasteromers, epimers, cyclicstructures of monosaccarides, mutarotation, reactions of monosaccarides, reducing and nonreducing sugars, chain-shortening andlengthening of sugars, proof of configuration, determinationof ring size, disaccharides and polysaccharides. 10 hrs

To have understanding to identify, describe the structure and properties of, and relate the functions of major biomolecules (carbohydrates, aminoacids, proteins, nucleic acids).

To gain understanding on applying fundamental concepts of organic chemistry, including stereochemistry, and reactivity of simple organic molecules to biological systems.

To have understanding to relate the structure of biomolecules to their properties and functions.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ER5371 : Structural Geology Laboratory { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Outcrop Patterns and Structure Contours - Trigonometric solutions, Structure contours, The three-point problem, Determining outcrop patterns with structure contours.
Module 2: Interpretation of Geologic Maps and structures - Determining exact attitudes from outcrop patterns, stratigraphic thickness in flat terrain and on slopes, Determining the nature of contacts, Constructing a stratigraphic column, Structure sections of folded layers and intrusive bodies, Drawing a topographic profile.
Module 3: Stereographic Projection - Pole of a plane, Line of intersection of two planes, True dip from strike and apparent dip, Rotation of lines, Fold classification based on dip isogons, Outcrop patterns of folds, Beta (ß) and Pi (p) diagrams, Determining the orientation of the axial plane.
Module 4: Dynamic and Kinematic Analysis of Faults - Measuring slip, Rotational (scissor) faulting, Map patterns of faults, Timing of faults, Dynamic analysis, Kinematic analysis, Structural synthesis of the Bree Creek, Common errors in geologic reports.
Module 5: Brittle Failure and Strain Measurement - Quantifying two-dimensional stress, The Mohr diagram, The Mohr circle of stress, The failure envelope, The importance of pore pressure, Longitudinal strain, Shear strain, The strain ellipse, Three strain fields, The coaxial deformation path and strain ellipse, Noncoaxial strain, The noncoaxial total strain ellipse, Strain in three dimensions, Quantifying the strain ellipsoid.

Course Objective

1 .

Understanding Geological Mapping and Structural Contours – Develop proficiency in using trigonometric solutions, structure contours, and outcrop pattern analysis for structural interpretation.
2 .

Interpreting Geologic Maps and Structural Relationships – Gain expertise in measuring rock attitudes, stratigraphic thickness, and constructing cross-sections and stratigraphic columns.
3 .

Applying Stereographic Projection Techniques – Use stereographic projection to analyze structural orientations, fold classifications, and axial plane orientations.
4 .

Conducting Fault Kinematics and Structural Synthesis – Perform dynamic and kinematic fault analysis, including slip measurements and fault timing assessments.
Analyzing Stress and Strain in Geological Structures – Utilize Mohr diagrams, strain ellipses, and failure criteria to evaluate brittle deformation and strain in three dimensions.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. To develop skills in geological mapping, structure contouring, and outcrop analysis.
2. To interpret geologic maps and create accurate cross-sections for structural investigations.
3. To apply stereographic projection techniques for structural geology problem-solving.
4. To analyze faults dynamically and kinematically, integrating structural synthesis.
5. To perform stress and strain analysis for understanding rock deformation and failure.

Essential Reading

1 .

S. K. Ghosh, Structural Geology: Fundamentals and modern development, Pergamon , 1st edition, 1993

2 .

N.W Gokhale, A Manual Of Problems In Structural Geology, CBSPD

Supplementary Reading

John Waldron and Morgan Snyder, Geological Structures: a Practical Introduction, University of Alberta Library

8782.t: FP4401: Hygienic Design of Equipment in Food Processing
8782.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : FP4401 : Hygienic Design of Equipment in Food Processing { 1-0-0 / 1}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Introduction to the importance of hygienic design, its historical evolution, and the microbiological risks associated with food processing, including contamination sources, biofilms, and pathogen control. The economic impact of poor hygienic design on productivity, recalls, and foodborne illness outbreaks is also discussed. Key international standards and regulations, such as EHEDG Guidelines , 3-A Sanitary Standards, ISO 14159, Codex Alimentarius, FDA’s Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs), and EU Regulations.
Materials of construction, FDA (21 CFR 177) and EU Framework Regulation (EC) Corrosion resistance, material compatibility (e.g., stainless steel, polymers, composites), cleanability, surface properties, and migration concerns (e.g., bisphenol A in polymers). Hygienic coatings, non-stick surfaces, self-polishing materials, and material selection criteria based on processing conditions (e.g., high-temperature, acidic, or high-fat foods).
The hygienic design principles. Cleanability, sanitization, and the avoidance of microbial harborage points. Eliminating dead spaces, cracks, and crevices, ensuring appropriate surface finish requirements, and designing hygienic welds, seals, and gaskets to prevent leakage and contamination. Structural design features such as self-draining systems, sloped surfaces, and open-frame construction.
The hygienic design principles for specific equipment, including tanks and vessels (interior finishes, access points), pumps and valves (aseptic connections, dead-leg prevention), heat exchangers (plate vs. tubular designs, fouling control), conveyors and belts (materials, modular belt hygiene, ease of disassembly), and filling and packaging machines (aseptic filling, sealing mechanisms, automated cleaning).
CIP (Clean-in-Place) and COP (Clean-out-of-Place), the selection and application of sanitizing agents, hygienic drain design, and self-draining equipment to minimize microbial growth. Validation methods like ATP bioluminescence testing and microbial swabbing, as well as biofilm formation, detection, and control strategies.
Regulations and standards, including EHEDG Guidelines, 3-A Sanitary Standards (applications in dairy, beverage, and pharmaceutical industries), ISO 14159, and the FDA Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA). Case studies of compliance and non-compliance with hygienic design standards.
Design and assessment, introducing risk assessment methodologies (e.g., HACCP-based assessments, FMEA), simulation and modeling tools.

Course Objective

1 .

To explain the fundamental principles of hygienic design and their role in ensuring food safety and regulatory compliance, with a focus on EU and international export requirements.
2 .

To analyze material selection, equipment design, and sanitation requirements to minimize microbial risks and enhance cleanability in food processing equipment.
3 .

To interpret and apply key international standards and guidelines (EHEDG, 3-A, ISO 14159) in the evaluation and design of hygienic food processing systems.
4 .

To develop practical skills in hygienic equipment design and assessment, enabling students to contribute to the global competitiveness of Indian food equipment manufacturers.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Describe and apply hygienic design principles to prevent food contamination and ensure compliance with international food safety standards.
2. Select and justify appropriate materials and design food processing equipment for easy cleaning, sanitization, and maintenance.
3. Interpret and implement relevant international standards and regulations (EHEDG, 3-A) for designing and evaluating hygienic food processing equipment.
4. Design and assess hygienic food processing equipment for specific applications, demonstrating an understanding of engineering principles and regulatory requirements for global market access.

Essential Reading

J. Holah and H.L.M. Lelieveld, Hygienic Design of Food Factories, Woodhead Publishing

2 .

John A. Troller, Sanitation in Food Processing, Academic Press

Supplementary Reading

1 .

EHEDG, EHEDG Guideline Documents, EHEDG

2 .

3-A Sanitary Standards, 3-A Sanitary Standards, Inc, 3-A Sanitary Standards

Journal and Conferences

Food Control, Elsevier
2 .

Journal of Food Protection, Elsevier
